Pecos Reservoirs · Management & Reuse Lab

Companion to the Salinity Lab Real data 2000–2020 SWAT+ gwflow · Pecos_USA

Interactive tool for thinking through where reuse water (treated oilfield produced water, or recycled municipal water) could go along the Pecos River, using the real management history of the 5 major dams — Santa Rosa, Sumner, Brantley, Avalon, and Red Bluff — between New Mexico and Texas. In Flow & Management you can test your own release policy for any dam (or try a one-click scenario) and watch the river — drawn as a single connected line through all 5 dams — light up or go dark; in Where to Place Reuse Water that same river diagram turns green/yellow/red so you can click a stretch directly. Once the SWAT+/gwflow model of the Pecos is finished, the simplified "dilution capacity" indicator here will be replaced by reach-by-reach simulated salt transport from the Salinity Lab, closing the loop between reservoir management and optimal reuse siting.

2. Real gages, and where GDROM actually fits

Everywhere else in this lab, "release" for 4 of the 5 dams is a blend: mostly GDROM (a New Mexico Interstate Stream Commission model — trained on storage, inflow-by-mass-balance, drought index, and day-of-year, not a direct measurement) for part of the period, with a real USGS downstream gage filling the rest. Correction, checked against the project's own calibration package (README_calibration.md): GDROM isn't a workaround to avoid — the project's own guidance is to use the GDROM_obs rows as the highest-quality reference for release calibration, since it's trained on actual reservoir operations, not a raw downstream gage with its own noise. What's genuinely missing that this lab adds is the real, independent inflow gage for each reservoir — GDROM's own "inflow" is not measured, it's back-calculated from storage change + release — so pairing GDROM's release with these real inflow gages gives you an actual, independent water-balance check that didn't exist before.

Below: every real USGS streamgage we could find upstream (inflow) and downstream (outflow) of each of the 5 dams, plus each reservoir's own storage/elevation gage — already plotted on the map above — with period-of-record and how to use each one. inflow   outflow (in use)   outflow, flagged/no data   storage   storage, better alternative   basin context

Recommended calibration/validation split (from the project's calibration package): simulation runs 2000–2020 with a 2000–2004 warmup (outputs start 2005). Calibrate on 2005–2017 (where all observed storage series overlap) and hold out 2018–2020 for validation — Red Bluff's storage record is the exception, it runs the full 2000–2020 with no gaps.

4. Download real data, ready for SWAT+/gwflow

All 17 series below are real daily USGS/observed records (2000-01-01 to 2020-12-31, or whatever period the gage actually has) at native daily resolution — the same source files behind the GDROM-blended monthly numbers used elsewhere in this lab, just not yet monthly-aggregated. If you're running SWAT+/gwflow with daily output for calibration, use these directly rather than re-deriving daily values from the monthly charts. Each reservoir has up to three roles: inflow (upstream gage), outflow (downstream/release gage), and storage (reservoir pool gage). The .day files match the recall.rec daily-recall format your SWAT+ project already uses for Red Bluff (year jday flo(m3/s) sed orgn sedp no3 solp chla nh3 no2 cbod dox san sil cla sag lag grv, constituents zeroed — fill in if you have them). Flow is in m³/s; storage is in acre-feet, USGS convention.

5. How to use this for SWAT+/gwflow calibration

⚠ Red Bluff data-quality flag, updated — read this first. The gage this lab (and the underlying SWAT+ model) uses as Red Bluff's "release," 08407500 "Pecos River at Red Bluff, NM," sits about 19 km (12 mi) north of the actual dam — still in New Mexico. The geometrically correct gage right below the dam, 08410100 "Pecos Rv below Red Bluff Dam near Orla, TX," exists but has zero continuous discharge record (only discrete water-quality samples, 1959–1969) — so no gage anywhere measures the dam's actual regulated release. We checked whether Texas has something better: TWDB and waterdatafortexas.org only publish storage for Red Bluff (themselves sourced from USGS 08410000, already listed below) — no separate TX release dataset exists. But the official Pecos River Compact River Master annual report (a U.S. Supreme Court-ordered interstate accounting, Case No. 65 Original) confirms 08407500 is the officially recognized New Mexico→Texas delivery-accounting gage for this river — not an ad hoc workaround, it's the legal measurement point. That same report also lists a second component of "historical outflow" we were missing: 08408500 "Delaware River near Red Bluff, NM," a real tributary that joins the Pecos between 08407500 and the dam (now on the map above). Bottom line: 08407500 + Delaware River together are the best real approximation of total inflow reaching Red Bluff Reservoir — still not the same thing as "regulated release for irrigation," which has no direct gage. For storage, 08410000 "Red Bluff Reservoir near Orla, TX" has a real daily record back to 1937 — likely more defensible than the TWDB Word/Excel documents this lab currently uses for Red Bluff storage.
Water-balance calibration check, per reservoir, per time step:
Inflow − Outflow − ΔStorage ≈ Evaporation + Seepage + ungauged tributary/return flow
Compute this from the real gages above (not the GDROM blend) and compare it to what SWAT+/gwflow actually simulates for that same reservoir — gwflow_flux_resv is the model's own reservoir–aquifer exchange output, and the reservoir's hydrology.res evap_co term drives the evaporation term. A large, systematic residual is a real calibration signal (missing seepage, an uncounted diversion, or the wrong evap coefficient) — not just noise from swapping GDROM for gage data.
How the model actually uses this data (per README_calibration.md): recall_res.rec/.dat in TxtInOut/ already carries the assembled observed release series, but it feeds in as an additional flow input — it does not replace the reservoir's own internal routing. To impose observed releases directly instead of letting SWAT+ compute them, you'd have to redirect the reservoir.con outlet connections to the recall elements — a real model-structure change, best treated as a separate diagnostic run, not the default calibration path. The real inflow gages here are best used as an independent check layered on top: compute the water balance above from real gages, then compare the residual to what gwflow_flux_resv reports for that reservoir.
The actual parameters to adjust (hydrology.res, method drawdown_days): shp_co1 (target storage fraction, wet season, suggested range 0.4–0.9) and shp_co2 (dry season, 0.1–0.6). Current values in this model — none are inside the suggested range yet, so this is genuinely a starting point, not a finished calibration:
Reservoirshp_co1 (current)shp_co2 (current)
Santa Rosa0.1160.081
Sumner0.2100.147

The reservoir's hydraulic geometry (vol_ps, area_ps, vol_es — principal/emergency spillway storage and area) was set from official USACE National Inventory of Dams data and should not be changed during calibration — only the two shape coefficients above. Fit shp_co1/shp_co2 per reservoir against observed monthly storage (NSE or KGE — daily is too noisy), then validate the resulting simulated release against the gages here.

Once you've run the model, these are the exact output files/columns to compare against the real data on this page: reservoir_mon.txt column vol_m3 (÷1,233.48 → acre-feet, compare to storage gages) · channel_mon.txt / channel_day.txt column flo_out (m³/s, compare to release/inflow gages) · gwflow_cell_stats.out column head (m, compare to the 70 observation wells in section 6 below) · basin_wb_mon.txt columns perc/surq for a basin-wide water-balance sanity check.

6. Groundwater wells — the calibration target this lab was missing

Streamflow calibration alone is not a SWAT+/gwflow calibration. Everything above (sections 1–5) only checks the surface-water side. gwflow is a coupled surface–groundwater model — fitting reservoir release/storage without also checking simulated heads against real wells can hide a badly wrong aquifer (K, storage coefficient, boundary conditions) that happens to still route the right amount of water downstream. 60 real observation wells — 23 USGS NWIS (param 72019, depth to water) + 37 TWDB Groundwater Database — are shown below, all crosswalked to a gwflow grid cell in this project's own obs_wells_catalog_v2.csv / gwflow.obs, and all confirmed inside the real SWAT+ watershed boundary (point-in-polygon test against the project's own subs1.shp subbasin delineation, not just the grid's bounding rectangle).
Toggle "Observation wells" on the map above (Groundwater wells group) to see all 60 — click any well for its real hydrograph (head in meters above mean sea level; higher = shallower water table).
What a consultant would still flag before trusting these as calibration targets:
  • 10 of the original 70 wells (all USGS) were dropped — real data, but outside the modeled basin. The obs_wells/ folder has 70 wells; only 60 are in this project's own crosswalk. Fitting the missing 10 to the 2000 m grid by regression (done in an earlier pass) placed all 10 inside the grid's bounding rectangle — but a point-in-polygon test against the real subs1.shp watershed delineation showed all 10 fall outside the actual irregular watershed shape — one sits well south of Red Bluff near the Big Bend region (30.36°N), others sit east/northeast of the Pecos, beyond the basin divide (e.g. toward the Llano Estacado / High Plains, consistent with several of them showing a High Plains/Ogallala local aquifer code rather than the Pecos Valley/Roswell Basin unit gwflow models). That's almost certainly why the project's own catalog excluded them in the first place. Removed from the map, the table, and every download.
  • Well depth is in the table for 22 of the remaining 23 USGS wells (fetched live from the NWIS site service — well_depth_va — plus each well's raw local aquifer code, shown in its popup, not decoded to a plain name here). TWDB depth/construction data was not pulled this pass — TWDB's groundwater database doesn't expose a simple batch API the way NWIS does; each of the 37 wells' report page would need to be fetched individually. Depth alone doesn't prove it's the right aquifer — cross-check the local aquifer code against the model's own gwflow/input_files/ra_43RSWLBS_top/bot.tif (aquifer #43 "Roswell Basin" top/bottom surfaces, the unit this gwflow model's thickness/K rasters are actually built from) before trusting any single well.
  • Record length is very uneven — from 12 readings (barely usable) to 8,751 (near-daily telemetry). Weight wells by record quality in any formal objective function, don't treat all 60 equally.
  • This lab visualizes and exports targets — it does not calibrate. Real inverse calibration for a joint surface+groundwater objective (reservoir storage/release and well heads, simultaneously, not sequentially) needs PEST/PEST++ or SWAT+ Toolbox/SWATplusR wrapping the actual model run — this page can hand those tools clean, sourced target series, nothing more.
  • Soft data this basin still has none of: remote-sensing ET (OpenET/MODIS) for basin-wide water-balance closure, and any real spring-discharge record for an independent groundwater–surface-water exchange check — both standard SWAT+ soft-calibration targets, both absent from this project so far.

5. Or adjust each dam by hand

What these controls mean:
  • Custom rule — turn this on for a dam to test a different way it could be operated, instead of exactly what happened historically. Leave it off to keep using the real record for that dam.
  • Scale — how much more or less water that dam releases each month, as a percent of what it actually released historically. 100% = no change. 150% = one-and-a-half times as much every month. 50% = half as much.
  • Min. floor — a guaranteed minimum amount of water that dam must release every month, no matter how dry it gets — even in months when it historically released almost nothing. This works like a minimum-instream-flow rule that protects the river downstream.

Turning on the rule for one dam only changes the river reach right below that dam (and everything further downstream, until the next dam re-regulates the water). Turning on several dams at once lets you test a whole basin-wide policy — for example, guaranteeing a minimum flow everywhere.

How often would this reach be risky? (full 2000–2020 record)

Instead of looking at just one month, this uses the full 252 months of real data for the chosen reach to count how often your proposed volume would exceed different flow thresholds — i.e., how often this site would have had little dilution capacity. The chart below always reflects your current rule settings (historical if you haven't changed anything).
How to read this: a "good" reuse site is one where the % of months in the red zone is low — a reach with high, stable flow most of the year. A reach that turns red often (especially in 2011–2013, or in summer) needs a smaller reuse volume, additional treatment, relocation downstream of a dam with steadier releases, or a minimum-release rule on the upstream dam — try setting a floor on the Flow & Management tab and watch these numbers change.
Exactly how is this computed?

For each of the 252 months with valid data: ratio = (reuse_volume/12) / dam_release_that_month. The dam release is the observed historical value, or your custom rule's output for that dam if you've enabled one — either way it's the release of the dam immediately upstream of that reach (for the reach below Red Bluff, Red Bluff's own release/rule is used as a lower bound — there are unmeasured additional inflows further downstream, so the real risk there is likely lower than shown).

Green = ratio < 2% (high dilution). Yellow = 2–10% (moderate). Red = >10%, or flow ≈ 0 (minimal or no dilution).

This is a water-quantity proxy, not a salt-transport model — it does not account for background concentration, mixing time, or river–aquifer exchange. That step belongs to the Salinity Lab (SWAT+/gwflow).

Where does this water actually go? Quality + the real irrigation network

Everything above treats "risk" as a quantity question — is there enough river flow to dilute the reuse volume. But dilution isn't really the goal for well-treated water: if the treated water is genuinely good quality (post-desalination TDS/organics/ammonia at or below the receiving reach's background — see the TxPWC pilot testing data, Sources tab), then discharging it where natural flow is low isn't necessarily bad — it can be the opposite: it's water that reach didn't have, going to a stretch that needs it, as long as it actually reaches a real use downstream instead of just evaporating in a low-flow, high-evaporation reach. That's where the real irrigation canal network (new toggleable layer on the Map tab, "Canals & ditches", 305 real USGS NHD features) matters: a good discharge site is upstream of, and close to, a real diversion, not just anywhere the flow number looks favorable.

The Pecos is already a salty river — before adding anything

Much of the Pecos basin in New Mexico and Texas crosses Permian evaporite formations (Rustler and Salado): salt and gypsum that groundwater dissolves as it circulates. Where that saline water surfaces or connects with the river — notably at Malaga Bend, about 18 miles southeast of Carlsbad, NM — the river receives a documented natural brine load far above background.

Documented brine source — Malaga Bend. USGS studies attribute the salinity here to brine leaking upward from a confined aquifer at the base of the Rustler Formation, mixing with fresher shallow groundwater and discharging to the Pecos at roughly 0.5 cubic feet per second of saturated brine in this reach — enough to measurably raise river TDS. USGS field-tested a brine-diversion approach here decades ago under the Malaga Bend Experimental Salinity Alleviation Project, one of the earliest documented attempts to intervene in the Pecos's natural salt budget.
Fish don't see it the same everywhere. The Pecos pupfish (Cyprinodon pecosensis) — a fish found only in the Pecos drainage — currently persists in the upper basin, from Bitter Lake National Wildlife Refuge (near Roswell, NM) down to just north of Brantley Reservoir. It has been eliminated from the middle and lower Pecos, including the reach through Malaga Bend and Red Bluff, where high natural salinity is one of the documented pressures. In November 2024, the U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service proposed listing it as Threatened under the Endangered Species Act, with critical habitat covering about 136 river miles and 26,555 acres across New Mexico and a Texas population in Salt Creek — not yet finalized as of this writing.

This tab is informational: exact brine flow rates, remediation outcomes, and the final ESA listing/critical-habitat status should be verified against the official sources below before being used in a report or decision — the point here is that whoever plays with this map knows the salinity problem, and the fish response to it, are real and already documented.

Why this doesn't compute salt (yet)

This lab uses real flow (Mm³/month released by each dam) as a proxy for dilution capacity. It doesn't move TDS, doesn't know whether a reach is gaining or losing groundwater, and doesn't know the background salt load in each reach.

That's exactly what the Salinity Lab (gwflow + SWAT+) does: advection–dispersion transport of TDS, river–aquifer exchange via streambed conductance, and comparison against EPA/agricultural/livestock thresholds.

The integration plan: once the SWAT+/gwflow model of the Pecos (346×227 cells, 2 km) is calibrated using these same observed releases as its flow forcing, every reach between dams will have a simulated TDS concentration. That number replaces the "% of flow" indicator in the previous tab with a real result: how much reuse water a reach can actually take without exceeding the TDS threshold that affects the Pecos pupfish or downstream uses.

Official storage capacity per dam (public record)

These figures are the publicly documented design/storage capacities, not the 2000–2020 observed maximum used for the live "% of storage" gauges elsewhere in this lab. Red Bluff release investigation — what we checked

  • Pecos River Compact — Report of the River Master, Water Year 2023 (Accounting Year 2024). U.S. Supreme Court Case No. 65, Original, Amended Decree. Table 1 (B.1.c) confirms USGS 08407500 "Pecos River at Red Bluff, NM" as the official New Mexico→Texas delivery-accounting gage, combined with 08408500 (Delaware River) and a small metered canal diversion (Permit 3254) as the compact's "Total Annual Historical Outflow."
  • USGS 08408500 — Delaware River near Red Bluff, NM (32.0231°N, 104.0545°W) — real tributary gage, daily discharge Oct 1937–present, joins the Pecos between 08407500 and the dam.
  • waterdatafortexas.org — Red Bluff Reservoir (TWDB's public portal) — checked directly: publishes storage/elevation only (sourced from USGS 08410000, already listed above), no separate release/outflow dataset for Texas.
  • TWDB — Red Bluff Reservoir summary page — descriptive/physical data only, links out to waterdatafortexas.org for anything operational.

Model GIS layers on the map (subbasins, river network, LSU)

  • Pulled directly from the SWAT+ project's own delineation output: Watershed/Shapes/subs1.shp (309 subbasins), rivs1.shp (2,405 channel reaches), lsus1.shp (Landscape Units — Floodplain/Upslope per channel).
  • All three are natively in EPSG:32613 (WGS 84 / UTM zone 13N, the model's working CRS) — reprojected to WGS84 lat/lon with pyproj for display here.
  • Geometry is simplified for the web with an iterative Douglas–Peucker algorithm (subbasins ≈385 m tolerance, river ≈165 m, LSU ≈440 m) — real shapes, not schematics, but not survey-precision either. At basin scale (Santa Rosa to Red Bluff is ~400 km) this is imperceptible.
  • LSU polygons are frequently split into many small disconnected fragments (some subbasins' floodplain LSU has 100+ separate slivers) — fragments smaller than roughly 650 m across after simplification are dropped as invisible at this zoom, cutting 4,783 raw LSU polygons down to the 3,776 shown without changing what you'd actually see on screen.
  • The 5 dam marker positions were switched from the SWAT+ reservoir.con object centroid (which can sit up to ~1.3 km from the real channel — it's the reservoir polygon's centroid, not a channel point) to the real USGS storage-gage coordinates at each dam, so they now line up with the real river layer.

Irrigation canal network + produced-water discharge context

  • The "Canals & ditches" map layer (305 features) is a live query of the USGS National Hydrography Dataset (NHDPlus High Resolution, hydro.nationalmap.gov/arcgis/rest/services/NHDPlus_HR/MapServer, layers 3 "NetworkNHDFlowline" + 4 "NonNetworkNHDFlowline"), filtered to FType=336 (Canal/Ditch) within a bounding box covering Reeves, Loving, Ward, and Pecos counties, TX — the area actually served by canals below Red Bluff. This is independent of the SWAT+ model, which does not represent irrigation canals/pipes as features — it's real infrastructure geometry, not a model layer.
  • Named canals returned by the query (shown in popups) include the Reeves County Water Improvement Canal, Barstow Canal, Giffin Canal, Main Canal, Highline Ditch, and several numbered laterals — consistent with the Red Bluff Water Power Control District, formed in 1927 from seven existing irrigation districts, which has used Red Bluff Reservoir to irrigate roughly 145,000 acres across Reeves, Loving, Pecos, and Ward counties since 1936. No public GIS polygon of the district's exact service-area boundary was found — only these real canal centerlines.
  • Red Bluff SWD Facility (🏭 marker, 31.893°N, 103.952°W): TCEQ TPDES Permit Application No. WQ0005445000 (NGL Water Solutions Permian, LLC — EPA ID TX0145289; NORI issued Dec 12, 2023; administratively complete, in technical review as of Aug 2026) — proposes discharging up to 16.9 million gal/day of filtered + desalinated produced water via Outfall 001 directly into Red Bluff Reservoir. Also see reporting in Inside Climate News (Aug 20, 2026) and Texas Public Radio (Aug 23, 2026), which also cover the smaller Texas Pacific Water Resources pilot facility near Orla, Reeves County (10,000 bbl/day = 420,000 gal/day, discharging to Salt Creek, a Pecos tributary — not directly to Red Bluff Reservoir, and not mapped separately here).
  • Treatment-quality evidence (referenced in the Reuse tab's "Where does this water actually go?" panel, not re-derived here): TxPWCPilotTestingWaterQualityReport.md (TxPWC Produced Water Treatment Pilot Testing: Water Quality Report, 2026-04-21) — 60 samples from 5 Permian Basin pilot projects; thermal and membrane desalination pilots "successfully removed" most TDS, with some trace organics/metals persisting through post-treatment polishing. This lab does not have a per-reach or per-month water-quality time series, so it does not compute a quantitative quality score — the note is qualitative and points to this report as the evidentiary basis.

Groundwater observation wells

  • The gwflow/input_files/obs_wells/*.csv folder has 70 wells (92,933 readings, 2000-01-01 to 2026-08-17): 33 from USGS NWIS groundwater (parameter 72019, depth to water) and 37 from the TWDB Groundwater Database. Only the 60 wells already in this project's own obs_wells_catalog_v2.csv/gwflow.obs crosswalk are used here — a point-in-polygon test of the other 10 (all USGS) against the real Watershed/Shapes/subs1.shp subbasin delineation (not just the gwflow grid's bounding rectangle) confirmed they sit outside the modeled watershed, which is almost certainly why the project's own crosswalk already excluded them. Monthly-averaged here (4,374 well-months across the 60 kept wells) to keep the file light — raw daily/sub-daily readings stay in the source CSVs.
  • Well depth (well_depth_va) and local aquifer code (aqfr_cd) for the 23 remaining USGS wells came from a live USGS NWIS site service query (siteOutput=expanded), fetched this session — available for 22 of 23. The 37 TWDB wells have no depth/construction data pulled yet — TWDB's Groundwater Database doesn't expose a simple batch API for this the way NWIS does.
  • head_m_amsl is meters above mean sea level, computed from each site's depth_to_water_ft and land-surface elevation — directly comparable to gwflow's own gwflow_cell_stats.out head column once the model is run.

How the data was aggregated for this lab

  • The daily CSVs (~7,671 days × 5 dams) were aggregated to monthly totals/averages (252 months) to keep the file light and easy to explore — the full daily detail is still available in gwflow/input_files/obs_reservoir/ for finer analysis.
  • Monthly release is the sum of that month's daily m³, converted to Mm³. Monthly storage is the mean of that month's observed acre-feet (af).
  • "% of storage" in the Management tab uses each dam's own 2000–2020 observed maximum as the reference — not its certified design capacity, which is now shown separately above.
  • "Reach flow" in the Reuse tab uses the release of the dam immediately upstream of that reach as a proxy — it does not include unmeasured tributary inflow or irrigation return flow between dams, so it underestimates real available flow over long reaches.
  • The monthly release_Mm3 array behind the Flow & Management and Reuse tabs comes from obs_release_*.csv's own source column, which is itself a blend: USGS_gage_proxy (a real instrument reading) for some days, GDROM_obs (the New Mexico ISC operations model's estimate, no gage reading that day) for others. Per-month majority source is tracked in release_source and shown as a shaded band on the history charts (Flow & Management, section 3) — Red Bluff is 100% real gage; Santa Rosa is real gage 2000–2008 and 2020 (~47% of months); Sumner/Brantley/Avalon are real gage only 2000–2004 and 2020 (~29% of months). We checked whether swapping to gage-only data would be "more real" for the whole tool — it would, but at the cost of dropping to 29–47% coverage with large multi-year gaps, which would break the what-if editor and dilution-risk histogram for 3 of 5 dams most of the time. The continuous blend was kept as the default (it's also this project's own recommended calibration reference, per README_calibration.md), with the real/modeled distinction made visible instead of silently hidden.
  • Daily (not just monthly) release and storage for all 5 dams — the same 17-series dataset behind the Map tab's download table — is the exact same source (obs_release_*.csv/obs_storage_*.csv), just not monthly-aggregated; useful directly if you're running SWAT+/gwflow with daily output for calibration instead of re-deriving daily values from these monthly charts.

How the "what-if" release rules and scenarios work

  • The rule editor (Flow & Management tab) is not a hydrologic model — it's a simple policy calculator layered on the real observed record: your_release = max(floor, historical_release × scale), applied month by month, per dam.
  • It does not simulate reservoir storage, inflow, evaporation, or downstream re-regulation — a rule you set on one dam changes the flow shown in the reach immediately below it, but the tool does not attempt to model what the next dam downstream would then do with that extra or reduced water.
  • The 5 preset scenarios (buttons above the table) are illustrative starting points, not forecasts or recommendations — each just sets specific scale/floor values, described in plain language when you click it.
  • The river diagram's flow-mode colors use a fixed 0–30 Mm³/month scale for visual contrast; the risk-mode colors use the same low/moderate/high thresholds documented in the "Where to Place Reuse Water" tab's "Exactly how is this computed?" panel.

This file is a direct companion to pecos_salinity_stakeholder.html (Salinity Lab) and gwflow_salinity_lab.html, built for the same Pecos_USA model (SWAT+ rev.61.0.2, gwflow grid 346×227 @ 2 km).
